subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: A 25-year-old man has an elevated FSH level on hormonal evaluation. His physician explains that a hormone normally secreted by the Sertoli cells provides negative feedback on FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.
question: Which of the following is the Sertoli cell product that inhibits FSH release?
explanation_correct: Sertoli cells are the non–germ cells that line the seminiferous tubules (homologs of female granulosa cells). They secrete inhibin B, which selectively inhibits FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary. Thus reduced Sertoli cell function (eg, from increased temperature) lowers inhibin B and raises FSH.

explanation_incorrect.A: Androgen-binding protein, also from Sertoli cells, maintains high local testosterone in the tubules; it does not inhibit FSH.
explanation_incorrect.C: Testosterone is secreted by Leydig cells and feeds back mainly on LH (via hypothalamus and pituitary), not FSH directly.
explanation_incorrect.D: Müllerian inhibiting factor is produced by Sertoli cells but causes regression of Müllerian ducts; it does not regulate FSH.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aromatase converts testosterone and androstenedione to estrogens; it is an enzyme, not the FSH-inhibiting hormone.

educationalObjective: Recall that Sertoli cells secrete inhibin B, which provides negative feedback on FSH secretion.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: A researcher is studying the factors that maintain a high local concentration of testosterone within the seminiferous tubules — a concentration required for normal spermatogenesis even when serum testosterone is modest. A Sertoli cell product is responsible for retaining this androgen locally.
question: Which of the following best explains the high intratubular testosterone concentration?

options.text: Leydig cells secrete androgen-binding protein into the tubular lumen
Sertoli cells secrete inhibin B, which binds and concentrates testosterone
Testosterone is produced by germ cells within the seminiferous tubules
The blood-testis barrier actively pumps testosterone into the tubules
Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein, which maintains local testosterone levels

explanation_correct: Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), which binds testosterone and maintains a high local concentration within the seminiferous tubules and epididymis — essential for spermatogenesis. Leydig cells produce the testosterone (under LH stimulation), but ABP is the Sertoli cell product that retains it locally.

explanation_incorrect.A: Androgen-binding protein is secreted by Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells; Leydig cells secrete testosterone in response to LH.
explanation_incorrect.B: Inhibin B inhibits FSH secretion; it does not bind testosterone or maintain local androgen levels.
explanation_incorrect.C: Testosterone is produced by Leydig cells in the interstitium, not by germ cells inside the tubules.
explanation_incorrect.D: The blood-testis barrier (Sertoli tight junctions) isolates gametes from the immune system; it does not pump testosterone into the tubules.

educationalObjective: Distinguish Leydig cell testosterone production from Sertoli cell androgen-binding protein that maintains high local testosterone.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: A 26-year-old man developed autoimmune orchitis after a testicular injury exposed sperm antigens to his immune system. Normally, developing gametes are sequestered from immune surveillance by a specialized barrier within the seminiferous tubules.
question: This barrier is formed by which of the following?

options.text: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
The tunica albuginea surrounding the testis
The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubules alone

explanation_correct: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier. This barrier isolates developing gametes (which are antigenically distinct) from the immune system, preventing autoimmune attack. It is one of the key supportive functions of Sertoli cells, which also nourish developing spermatozoa.

explanation_incorrect.B: Leydig cells are endocrine cells in the interstitium; they are not joined by the tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier.
explanation_incorrect.C: The tunica albuginea is the fibrous capsule around the testis; it is not the immunologic barrier that isolates gametes.
explanation_incorrect.D: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubules is not the barrier; the barrier is specifically the Sertoli–Sertoli tight junctions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gap junctions between germ cells permit communication but do not form an immune-isolating barrier.

educationalObjective: Identify the blood-testis barrier as Sertoli–Sertoli tight junctions that protect gametes from autoimmune attack.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: A 22-year-old man has a left varicocele and an undescended (cryptorchid) right testis. Semen analysis shows oligospermia, and laboratory studies show decreased inhibin B with normal serum testosterone and LH.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Increased temperature destroys Leydig cells, lowering testosterone and raising LH
Varicocele increases FSH secretion directly, which suppresses spermatogenesis
Cryptorchidism raises inhibin B, which suppresses sperm production
Elevated temperature impairs temperature-sensitive Sertoli cells, reducing sperm production and inhibin B, while Leydig cell testosterone production is unaffected
Decreased inhibin B directly raises testosterone production by Leydig cells

explanation_correct: Sertoli cells are temperature sensitive: increased scrotal temperature (as in varicocele or cryptorchidism) reduces sperm production and inhibin B secretion. Leydig cells are endocrine cells whose testosterone production is unaffected by temperature, so testosterone and LH remain normal while inhibin B falls (and FSH rises by feedback). This matches the findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Leydig cell testosterone production is unaffected by temperature; testosterone and LH remain normal here, so this does not explain the findings.
explanation_incorrect.B: A varicocele does not directly raise FSH; the FSH change is secondary to reduced inhibin B feedback from temperature-impaired Sertoli cells.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cryptorchidism lowers, not raises, inhibin B because Sertoli cells are temperature sensitive; the decreased inhibin B is the expected finding.
explanation_incorrect.E: Inhibin B feeds back on FSH, not on Leydig cell testosterone production; decreased inhibin B raises FSH, not testosterone.

educationalObjective: Explain that heat (varicocele, cryptorchidism) impairs temperature-sensitive Sertoli cells, lowering sperm and inhibin B, while Leydig testosterone is unaffected.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: A 30-year-old man has low testosterone with elevated LH. His physician explains that a population of interstitial endocrine cells in the testes produces testosterone in response to LH and is the male homolog of the female theca interna cells.
question: Which cells are being described?
explanation_correct: Leydig cells are the endocrine cells in the testicular interstitium that secrete testosterone in the presence of LH. They are the homolog of the female theca interna cells. In primary hypogonadism, low testosterone with elevated LH indicates Leydig cell failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Sertoli cells are the non–germ cells lining the seminiferous tubules, respond to FSH, and are the homolog of granulosa cells, not theca interna.
explanation_incorrect.B: Spermatogonia are germ cells that maintain the germ pool and produce primary spermatocytes; they do not secrete testosterone.
explanation_incorrect.D: Granulosa cells are the female homolog of Sertoli cells and are not present in the male testis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Endothelial cells line blood vessels and do not produce testosterone.

educationalObjective: Identify Leydig cells as the LH-responsive interstitial endocrine cells that secrete testosterone (homolog of theca interna).

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Seminiferous tubules: Sertoli and Leydig cells
vignette: During male fetal development, a testicular cell product causes regression of the Müllerian ducts, preventing development of the uterus and fallopian tubes. The same cell type later supports spermatogenesis in the adult testis by nourishing developing sperm and forming the blood-testis barrier.
question: Which of the following is the cell type and product responsible?
explanation_correct: Sertoli cells (non–germ cells, homologs of granulosa cells) produce Müllerian inhibiting factor (MIF), which causes regression of the Müllerian ducts in the male fetus. In the adult, the same Sertoli cells support and nourish developing sperm, secrete inhibin B and androgen-binding protein, and form the blood-testis barrier via tight junctions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Leydig cells secrete testosterone in response to LH, which supports Wolffian duct development, not Müllerian regression.
explanation_incorrect.B: Inhibin B is secreted by Sertoli cells and inhibits FSH; germ cells do not secrete it, and it does not cause Müllerian regression.
explanation_incorrect.C: Leydig cells do not produce MIF; MIF is a Sertoli cell product.
explanation_incorrect.D: Androgen-binding protein is a Sertoli cell product that maintains local testosterone; spermatogonia are germ cells and do not secrete it.

educationalObjective: Recall that Sertoli cells produce Müllerian inhibiting factor for fetal Müllerian duct regression and later support spermatogenesis.
